extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors and essayists; readers interested in moral/philosophical writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing moral/philosophical essays aimed at public readership — covering style, usefulness, audience, and the author's conduct. Emphasizes clarity, perseverance, social responsibility, and the moral purpose of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral usefulness / purpose of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of morality are useful because they inculcate and preserve knowledge and virtue even if their influence is gradual and imperceptible; the labours of the moralist are not vain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that though a single book may not visibly reform cities or nations, moral instruction contributes slowly to civilization's improvement; authors should therefore write with the aim of inculcating virtue and not be discouraged by the lack of immediate, observable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and accessibility of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often more successful to propagate truth by explaining it clearly than by abstruse, subtle speculation: 'truth is often more successfully propagated by men of moderate abilities, who... explain them clearly'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor lucid exposition and accessibility over demonstration of intellectual virtuosity; writers who make ideas reachable to receptive readers can have greater practical influence than abstruse theorists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful choice of words and euphony
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, therefore, as well as things, claim the care of an author; authors may labour over single words, hesitate between expressions, and even 'run from one end of Paris to the other' to test a period on a 'nice ear'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay close attention to diction, rhythm, and the sound of sentences; revise repeatedly to remove awkward repetitions and to select terms that accurately and pleasingly render thought (examples in the text: changing a sentence for repeated letters, consulting friends' ears).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence, steady perseverance, and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition is for the most part 'an effort of slow diligence and steady perseverance' rather than perpetual rapture; many passages require long study and repeated rewriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and accept that writing requires hard work: sustained attention, reordering confused thoughts, untangling labyrinthine ideas, and persistent revision to reach clarity and finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience awareness and tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers read for different ends (style, argument, amusement, to shine in conversation, to avoid appearing ignorant); 'Some read for style, and some for argument.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider readers' motives and tailor aspects of the work (style, depth, examples, tone) to the intended audience; be mindful that different readers will value different qualities in the same work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of providing innocent amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: The author is 'not wholly useless, who provides innocent amusements' for those who turn to books as refuge or pastime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that entertaining writing has social worth; balancing instruction with agreeable diversion helps keep minds from worse temptations and can be a legitimate writerly aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not neglect 'little things' and social manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation of knowledge from 'those weaknesses by which knowledge is generally disgraced' warns that learned men often neglect domestic affairs and common forms; 'the manners of the world... are not a regular system planned by philosophers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should attend to practical social forms and everyday manners; neglecting small civilities and forms of behaviour can undermine usefulness and invite contempt even when one possesses great learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contempt, arrogance, and facile negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Drollery, ridicule, contempt and arrogance are the easiest forms of wit and philosophy; to find objections to everything and laugh at the industrious without modelling superior activity is easy and petty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from mere sarcasm or dismissive criticism of others' occupations; constructive engagement or setting a better example is more virtuous than cynical contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity — avoid affectation except for moral necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Singularity (affecting oddness) is generally displeasing and often a mark of vanity; yet 'it is noble to dare to stand alone' in moral and religious questions where duty overrides fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt eccentricity as a badge of superiority; conform to social conventions when it aids usefulness and rapport, but be willing to be singular when conscience or moral truth requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match aims to personal powers — realistic scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A just estimate of one's actions is formed 'by making his power the test of his performance' — do what is great with respect to oneself rather than measuring by impossible visions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set ambitions and standards according to one's actual abilities; focus on faithfully performing tasks within one's competence rather than lamenting or aiming at impossibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination of work and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of asking 'What have I been doing?' — computing the loss and profit of undertakings and examining whether hours spent were applied to laudable purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly review and assess your own writing career and individual pieces: intentions, skill, and attainable ends; be prepared to judge whether work was useful or merely diversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance despite imperceptible immediate effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of every individual is small; 'the progress of reformation is gradual and silent... every drop increases the inundation' — authors' influence may be slow and largely unseen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain industry and confidence even if public impact is not immediately visible; the cumulative effect of many modest contributions matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting old truths freshly is valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: A man need not discover unknown truth to be useful; 'he may be sufficiently useful, by only diversifying the surface of knowledge, and luring the mind by a new appearance to a second view of those beauties' previously overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel presentation, clarification, and re-emphasis of established ideas are legitimate and valuable aims for writers; strive to illuminate rather than only to invent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using disdain as a cloak for idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal contempt and haughty negligence are 'often assumed by indolence when it disowns its name' — people may pretend to disdain activity to mask laziness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against performing rhetorical disdain while avoiding real effort; authentic greatness is shown by faithful exertion, not by affected loftiness.
